Nov 10 : Nscale, a British cloud provider backed by chip giant Nvidia, is considering delaying a $35 billion stock market listing, the Telegraph reported on Tuesday. Executives at the data-centre developer are assessing whether to pause efforts to go public until next year, the report added. Nscale did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours. The report comes days after Reuters reported that Microsoft had declined an option to expand its existing agreement with Nscale to rent more computing power at a Texas data center.

The London-based company filed for an IPO in September, when it sought about $3.5 billion in funding, including $2 billion from Nvidia. Nscale plans to list on the NYSE under the symbol "NSCL." The news about Nscale's IPO comes as Anthropic moves ahead with its own listing plans. The AI giant on Tuesday filed an updated prospectus for its IPO, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, slightly short of some investors' expectations. Anthropic's IPO is seen as a key test of Wall Street's faith in the AI boom it helped ignite.

MADRID, Nov 10 : Spain's government has demanded that TikTok suspend its operations in Spain until it eliminates child sexual abuse material, it said on Tuesday, after a media report documented 1,183 explicit posts on the platform with millions of views. Youth Minister Sira Rego, whose ministry cannot singlehandedly ban the platform in Spain, has appealed to prosecutors and the Data Protection Agency to take action against the social media company, according to a statement by the ministry. "Social media cannot be lawless territory," Rego said. The request comes months after Sanchez's government requested a probe into X, Meta and TikTok for allegedly spreading AI-generated child sexual abuse material, as European regulators intensify scrutiny of big tech over harmful and illegal content.

FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : US electricity consumption will rise to record highs in 2026 and 2027 due to power-hungry AI data centers and electrification, the US Energy Information Administration said in its Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) on Tuesday. The EIA projected that power demand will rise from a record 4,216 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2025 to 4,306 billion kWh in 2026 and 4,370 billion kWh in 2027. If correct, 2026 would be the third year in a row of record demand. Demand is surging largely due to data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence. Homes and businesses have also been relying more on electricity and less on fossil fuels for heat and transportation. The EIA forecast that power sales in 2026 will rise to 1,546 billion kWh for residential consumers, 1,557 billion kWh for commercial customers and 1,061 billion kWh for industrial customers.

The all-time highs stand at 1,519 billion kWh for residential consumers and 1,503 billion kWh for commercial customers in 2025 and 1,064 billion kWh for industrial customers in 2000. As renewable output rises, the EIA said the share of power generation from coal will slide from 17 per cent in 2025 to 15 per cent in 2026 and 2027, while the share of natural gas in 2026 will hold steady from 2025 at 40 per cent, then ease to 39 per cent in 2027. The percentage of renewable generation will rise from around 24 per cent in 2025 to 25 per cent in 2026 and 28 per cent in 2027, while nuclear power's share will hold at 18 per cent in 2026 and 2027, the same as in 2025, according to the outlook. The EIA projected that gas sales in 2026 would slide to 12.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) for residential consumers and 9.4 bcfd for commercial customers, but rise to 23.8 bcfd for industrial customers and 37.4 bcfd for power generation. Those figures compare with all-time highs of 14.3 bcfd in 1996 for residential consumers, 9.9 bcfd in 2025 for commercial customers, 23.8 bcfd in 1973 for industrial customers, and 36.8 bcfd in 2024 for power generation.

Source: Reuters

Nov 10 : Anthropic said on Tuesday it was bringing its Claude assistant to video conference platform Google Meet, as the company pushes to integrate AI deeper into everyday office work. Earlier in the day, Anthropic launched a roadshow for its highly anticipated US initial public offering, with plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion at a $1.02 trillion valuation. The offering will test investors' appetite for the AI boom and Anthropic's massive spending plans. Called Claude Meetings, the new feature will let users add Claude to video calls as a visible participant. Anthropic said Claude would be able to follow the conversation and turn discussions into work in real time, while also drafting plans, creating timelines and answering questions in the call's chat. The feature is designed to shift AI's role in meetings from simply recording or summarizing conversations to doing the work that follows from them while the discussion is still taking place, Anthropic said.

The rollout is part of a broader push by Anthropic to make Claude an active participant in knowledge work. Nov 10 : IBM said on Tuesday that it was ending US visa and green card sponsorship for a majority of roles in IBM Consulting, which employs more than 150,000 people. The move comes amid tight scrutiny of foreign tech hiring by Donald Trump's administration. Last month, it suspended Microsoft, Adobe and several major outsourcers, including Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services, from the Permanent Labor Certification process — a key step toward green cards for foreign workers. IBM Consulting has used US high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages, but participation has been declining for years, a company spokesperson told Reuters. It opted to end sponsorship for most such roles as skill availability and client needs have evolved, the spokesperson added.

WASHINGTON, Nov 10 : Alphabet's Google has agreed to additional privacy protections in the acquisition of employee data from defunct Spirit Airlines, a union representing employees said Tuesday. The agreement clears the way next week for approval of Google's $10 million deal to acquire Spirit data to train AI models. The union said it had won a more rigorous de-identification process than previously planned and added significant employee data will be excluded from the sale, including health and medical information. As part of Spirit's closure and asset liquidation, Google won an auction in August for data from emails, spreadsheets and calendars, as well as for marketing, productivity and operations. Spirit Airlines halted operations in May. A bankruptcy judge is now set to approve the deal next week.

The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA said the de-identified data will also be reviewed by an independent verification agent chosen in consultation with unions, and Google is prohibited from attempting to re-identify the data and is required to process it in a secure environment and treat it as confidential. A group of about 120 lawmakers raised concerns last month about the data sale. Last month, a privacy ombudsman recommended a US bankruptcy judge approve the deal after excluding passenger personal information from 97 million Spirit customers. The lawmakers, led by Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and Representative Steven Horsford, a Nevada Democrat, said the sale would include 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages and other employee records. Spirit Airlines said it was pleased to have reached a resolution with labor unions as it continueed to maximize value for its creditors. "We are grateful for the collaboration of Google, the consumer privacy ombudsman, our labor unions, and other key stakeholders who are engaging with us constructively on this sale," a spokesperson said. Google, which did not immediately comment Tuesday, said last month it did not want to acquire personal information. "We are not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit. The information will either be completely excluded or will be de-identified by an independent third party before Google receives any data," Google said last month.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 10 : Toyota Motor said on Tuesday it will bring its ultra-compact mini KEI trucks to the US market for fleet customers starting in the second half of 2027 as part of a limited rollout after President Donald Trump encouraged the move. A third of the 3.7 million new cars sold in Japan last year were mini, or "kei", cars — tiny vehicles that are not produced by American automakers. The KEI-01, which has a 660 cc three-cylinder engine and four-wheel drive, will be assembled at Toyota's plant in Indiana. Toyota will add 50 jobs and invest $34 million in the project. The right-hand-drive trucks measure just over 11 feet (3.35 m) in length and under 5 feet in width with a maximum speed of 25 miles per hour (40 kph). Toyota said the vehicle is designed to comply with federal low-speed vehicle safety requirements and initial distribution will focus on fleet customers rather than retail sales. Toyota also said it is relaunching its Scion in the US.

TAIPEI, Nov 10 : TSMC plans to invest up to $1 billion across leading AI developers Anthropic and OpenAI, highlighting the Taiwanese chipmaker's confidence in long-term demand for the technology even as concerns grow about soaring AI spending. The company is positioning itself to benefit not only from supplying AI infrastructure, but also from owning stakes in some of the industry's most influential developers. TSMC's board approved on Tuesday an investment of up to $500 million to acquire shares in Anthropic at its initial public offering price, and an investment of up to $500 million to acquire preferred stock in OpenAI. The move comes after Anthropic on Tuesday priced its initial public offering at $70 to $78 per share, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion in what would be one of the largest stock market debuts on record.

BERLIN, Nov 10 : German defence firm Helsing will present new artificial intelligence-based military targeting software on Wednesday, seeking to benefit from growing concerns among European governments about relying on US companies such as Palantir. After President Donald Trump's repeated threats to quit NATO, concerns over dependence on Washington and data sovereignty have fuelled resistance against US data analytics and defence software firm Palantir in parts of Europe. The company makes the best-known military AI system of its kind, the Maven Smart System, which has been deployed by the US, NATO commands and several NATO members. In the invitation to the Berlin presentation of its system, Helsing said it was "crucial that we be able to conduct precise reconnaissance, make the right decisions in the face of uncertainty, and act with precision on the battlefield, with autonomy and without dependencies: from Europe and for Europe".

The war in Ukraine has shown the value of AI tools in dramatically speeding up battlefield decision-making by rapidly processing and interpreting vast streams of data generated by drones, satellites and other sensors. PALANTIR INSISTS CUSTOMERS ARE IN FULL CONTROL Palantir has insisted its customers are in full operational control of the software that they buy from the company and that it does not have a "kill switch" to deactivate it remotely. Concerns over dependence on the US were exacerbated last month after speed restrictions for Ukraine's Starlink terminals hampered Kyiv's efforts to intercept Russian drones and forced some operations to be cancelled. In June, the Trump administration moved to block non-US residents from Anthropic's most advanced models, Mythos and Fable, on national security grounds, prompting the AI company to abruptly suspend access to the models globally. The ban was lifted later the same month, but European lawmakers still warn the episode showed that the US holds a "kill switch" over essential technologies that it is more than willing to use. The German military has made clear that, for now at least, it will not buy Palantir's Maven for its forces. The country is aiming to deploy its own AI-powered system from 2027, with full implementation expected in 2028.

MUNICH, Nov 10 : Dutch chipmaker Nexperia is "totally oversubscribed" as suppliers divert manufacturing capacity toward fast-growing AI data centres and away from the mature chips used in cars and industrial equipment, interim CEO Stefan Tilger told Reuters at the Electronica trade fair in Munich on Tuesday. Tilger said some competitors had shifted capacity away from the commodity semiconductors supplied by Nexperia, creating bottlenecks in parts of the automotive supply chain. "The automotive industry is suffering at the moment quite heavily," he said in an interview. STMicroelectronics CEO Jean-Marc Chery warned on Monday that foundries and chip-packaging companies were increasingly shifting resources away from products used in automotive and industrial applications.

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : Banks worldwide are trying to curb the soaring cost of AI agents as spending on the tokens that power them could easily reach 20 per cent of total labor costs, according to McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review. Responsibility for controlling AI-related spending has shifted to new teams that some banks call AI FinOps. Initially, banks sought to rein in costs with systems that directed employees to different AI models based on the complexity of their queries. "But those models are ineffective when AI agents are working, because they communicate with each other and tokens quickly add up," said Vik Sohoni, a senior partner at McKinsey and one of the report's authors, in an interview with Reuters. As a result, banks are becoming more selective about where they deploy agentic AI, focusing on areas with the strongest expected returns. Productivity-related savings are relatively easy to measure, but banks are increasingly looking at AI-driven revenue growth to determine where higher spending is justified, Sohoni said.

Customers are adopting AI much faster than previous technologies, according to the report. McKinsey expects AI agents to become widely used within three years, compared with the 5 to 10 years it took mobile internet to gain broad adoption. A McKinsey survey of 46,000 retail banking customers worldwide found that most already use AI to compare banking services, find higher-yield savings accounts and refinance or consolidate debt. Among AI users, 72 per cent said they would allow a banking agent to carry out one financial task, although they would cap autonomous approvals at $500. Meta's Muse agent was downloaded 5 million times in the US during its first 22 days after launch. While AI agents could help banks boost revenue and cut costs, they could also pressure profits by shifting deposits from non-interest-bearing accounts into higher-yielding accounts. So far, that impact has been limited because most banks block external AI agents from authorizing transactions within their systems.

Nov 10 : Anthropic's blockbuster IPO is set to give the company a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, marking a defining test of investor confidence in the AI boom it helped ignite. Reuters exclusively reported on Tuesday that Anthropic and some of its investors aim to sell shares in an indicative price band of between $70 and $78 per share. The company is launching the roadshow for a historic share sale that is expected to set a benchmark for the sector, following years of hype that fueled a massive influx of capital into AI companies. COMMENTS:

ART HOGAN, CHIEF MARKET STRATEGIST AT B RILEY WEALTH, NEW YORK "Anthropic is very well anticipated and the more we learn about it, the more we'll likely see it as a positive catalyst getting done this year. You just have to look at their revenue growth and what they've been able to do over the course of the last year. So the story is all about their revenue growth, very much like the SpaceX IPO was. I think the fact that it will be now publicly traded, we'll have more information on a regular basis about how they're actually doing and you know, how long it will take to turn that revenue growth into earnings growth." MICHAEL FIELD, CHIEF EQUITY STRATEGIST, MORNINGSTAR, AMSTERDAM "It's an attractive offering, ultimately. I think that's going to be reflected in investor demand. Maybe the timing has actually worked out pretty okay for this. The valuation that they were looking for has fallen. Initially, we're talking $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, and then $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, and now it's just over $1 trillion." A key number for them is that trillion figure. If they couldn't get it away for that, then they might hold off. But ultimately, in their mind, if they can get the first batch off at a trillion, then that's enough for them to get the ball rolling on this." PATRICK ARMSTRONG, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, PLURIMI WEALTH, LONDON "Anthropic has swung back to a loss, and it is not going public in as hot a market as it would have been if it had done so in the summer. I do not think the price it gets, or the implied market value, will drive the AI trade. But if it has a very disappointing IPO, that would take further wind out of the sails of the AI market. You have hyperscalers with negative free cash flow, and data-center demand is being questioned because of politics." Valuation for companies like this is more art than science. There are comparison points such as SpaceX, which has a significant AI component, and the hyperscalers, which have embedded AI and cloud-computing businesses. But it is still a leap of faith, because the company is years away from meaningful free cash flow, even in more optimistic scenarios." LUKAS MUEHLBAUER, ASSOCIATE, IPOX SCHUSTER, EDINBURGH "The latest growth figures justify taking a trillion-dollar valuation seriously, however, being the first major pure-play AI lab to go public, there aren't really any direct peers to compare against. The most important factor in valuing Anthropic is the cash it can ultimately generate from customers after funding model development and computing infrastructure. The key questions are how durable customer spending is and whether the economics of providing inference improve over time. Customer retention and the spending required to maintain a technological lead are particularly important." FIONA CINCOTTA, SENIOR MARKET ANALYST, CITY INDEX, LONDON "It's a little bit lower than an initial expectation around the 69 billion that was sent out earlier this morning, but that was then considered inaccurate. And I think given the volatility, concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week. This is actually fairly bullish and it's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there." IPEK OZKARDESKAYA, SENIOR ANALYST AT SWISSQUOTE BANK, GENEVA, SWITZERLAND "What we are seeing is essentially a reassessment of Anthropic's value in a more challenging AI environment. The company continues to post impressive growth, but investors are increasingly focused on the cost of generating that growth. The shift from a $2 trillion valuation to today's level reflects a change in focus from revenue growth alone to the significant financial commitments and spending required to sustain it." The timing of the IPO is notable because investors have become much more focused on the costs of the AI buildout than they were over the past few years. Political and regulatory uncertainties, along with a higher interest-rate environment, have also raised questions about future AI spending. As a result, many investors see Anthropic's IPO as an important test of appetite for AI-related investments." MICHAEL BAKER, HEAD OF UK PREMIUM CLIENTS AT CAPITAL.COM, LONDON "You've got to build a sustainable client base that is willing to pay those sizeable bills, both on the consumer side and among businesses, that's what Anthropic will have to sustain. At the same time, it has to keep up with the costs of chips and data centers while continuing to offer competitive models and outperform major Chinese rivals." It's a huge valuation, and I think it will take a lot to convince investors that it represents a fair price."

Source: Reuters

Nov 10 : Criminals repeatedly use the same fraudulent bank accounts to target multiple businesses, highlighting the industrial scale of payment fraud, Patrice Bouexel, president of French payment security firm Sis ID, told Reuters. Internal data from Sis ID shows that a single fraudulent bank account is used against an average of 34 companies in its network, allowing scammers to multiply the impact of each account they manage to open. Sis ID monitors bank account information for businesses in more than 190 countries and territories. As of late October, it had identified and blocked more than 14,000 fraudulent International Bank Account Numbers, or IBANs, this year. Bouexel said the scale of the activity pointed to organised criminal networks rather than isolated fraudsters. Many fraudulent traces originate from the Asia-Pacific region or Russia. Large-scale scam operations also exist in countries such as Myanmar, where some participants are forced to work under coercive conditions, Bouexel said. These groups often target wealthier economies and large corporations.

Sis ID cross-checks bank account details against multiple data sources and intelligence shared by companies in its network before payments are made. It said 36 per cent of its automated verification decisions were based on information contributed by other businesses within its network. Once suspicious activity is detected, fraudulent accounts can often be flagged in near real time, while more complex investigations may take several hours, Bouexel said when asked how quickly Sis ID could block an account suspected of fraudulent activity. The company said it helped protect hundreds of billions of euros in payments each year across industries from energy and automotive manufacturing to chemicals and pharmaceuticals.

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : Bond investors are growing more cautious on debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom, highlighting concerns over the expected efforts of a Democrat-controlled Congress to slow the pace of AI investment and data center expansion. US high-yield credit spreads widened to 348 basis points in last Thursday's stock-market swoon, ICE BofA US Corporate Index data showed. That was the highest since May 2025, just a month after President Trump imposed global tariffs. Spreads narrowed on Friday to 342 basis points. "The markets are definitely anxious right now. I wouldn't be surprised to see some continued volatility in both high yield and loans," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds in New York. While healthy corporate fundamentals continue to support the market, a deeper reassessment of AI-related risk could push credit spreads wider in both high-yield and investment-grade debt in anticipation of stricter regulations on this technology, analysts and portfolio managers said. Investment-grade spreads were at 93 basis points last Thursday, against 91 the previous session.

Democrats are already planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting AI systems and data center development when they take control of Congress in January. Republican President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology, but over the weekend, following a historic midterm loss for his party, he signaled openness to safeguards. "Appetite is more cautious and more discriminating," said Ali Hassan, portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management. "Political and regulatory scrutiny is prompting a review of credits up and down the chain, from developers to contractors to suppliers." MORE CAUTIOUS APPETITE Data center bonds, many of them concentrated in the BB and single-B tiers of the junk bond market, have come under fresh pressure in recent weeks, especially during the technology selloff. Single-B spreads widened 35 basis points to 367 basis points, leading the deterioration in the high-yield market, analysts said, and hitting their highest levels since March. Galaxy Helios Data Center bonds fell to 89.25 cents on the dollar on November 5, for instance, lifting yields to 13 per cent from the 9.875 per cent offered when Galaxy Digital's wholly owned unit sold the B+ rated debt in late July. "A slowdown in the AI buildout that hits the supply chain, power producers, electrical contractors, equipment and machinery, data center developers, all of these are going to have a second-order effect," said Peter Yanulis, multi-asset portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles. For investors, the larger concern is the potential impact of AI regulation on economic growth. Investment in artificial intelligence and the infrastructure underpinning it has been a major engine of US expansion, helping keep growth resilient this year despite broad uncertainties. "Any slowdown in the pace of data center development has the potential to materially slow overall business investment," said Abiel Reinhart, senior economist at J.P. Morgan. RELIEF FROM SUPPLY In the near term, some investors believe a slowdown is probably a healthy thing for the credit market and for AI companies themselves, as stricter AI regulations mean less bond issuance - which should help support prices. "We can expect a bit more relief from the open floodgates that we've experienced on the AI supply and the market can now digest this transition period over the next six to 12 months," said Loomis Sayles' Yanulis. While investors are reassessing longer-term growth expectations, they see little risk of an immediate pullback in borrowing or capital spending tied to projects already under construction. "The political and regulatory uncertainty could impact the later years, 2028-2030 (and later), but it is unlikely to significantly change the capex and issuance numbers for 2027 as many of those projects are already underway and capital commitments have been made," said Karen Choi, portfolio manager at Capital Group. While investors see little risk to near-term spending plans, many argue the bigger question is whether policy changes can meaningfully alter AI's long-term outlook. "AI is not going to slow down," said Ben Emons, chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors. "If it's going to slow down in Texas, it will pop up somewhere in another state and just continue."

Source: Reuters
